headline: Jigged the Wilmington Edge for Bigeye While the Troll Spread Picked Off Giants and White Marlin
subhead: A warm filament has held over the canyon for a week straight, and boats working both the troll and the drop cashed in on bigeye, giant bluefin, and a scattered white marlin bite.
body_markdown:
If you've only got one shot at the Wilmington this week, run offshore early and decide troll-or-chunk based on what the temp break looks like when you get there — don't lock in the plan on the ride out. The warm filament that's been sitting over the canyon for the better part of ten days is still in place, and it's still producing, but the fleet's split roughly down the middle between trolling the color change on the way out and dropping back to jig or chunk once they find bait stacked on the structure. Both have worked. Neither has been a guarantee.

We flagged this last week — said conditions looked set to hold as long as nothing tropical came through to disrupt the warm water sitting over the grounds, and that's exactly what's played out. No storm track has pushed close enough to mess with the setup, the eddy's held its shape, and the bite's stayed steady rather than spiking and dying like it can this time of year. That's the good news. The watch item hasn't changed either — any cooling trend or a shift in that filament could push the fish toward the canyon edges fast, so this isn't a set-it-and-forget-it pattern. Check the latest satellite or a fresh water-temp read before you commit to a spot.

The bite itself has been rated a strong week by anyone who's put gas in the tank for it. Bigeye tuna have been coming on the jig over the deeper structure inside the canyon — 250 to 350 feet on the sounder, working vertical jigs like the Nomad Vertrex or a knife jig in the 200-300 gram range on a fast retrieve through the marks. That's not a bite for a slow afternoon; it takes commitment to keep working the column until you find the right depth the fish are holding at, but boats that stuck with it have had multiple bigeye in the 100-150 pound class over a day's fishing.

On the troll side, giant bluefin have been the story, and they've been coming both on the spread and on the flat lines. Ballyhoo and cedar plugs pulled at 6-7 knots along the temp break has raised fish, but the better producer has been live-lining — a bunker or a big cigar minnow flat-lined off the corner while the rest of the spread works the break has been drawing strikes from giants that clearly want something moving natural, not something towing at trolling speed. That's a slower way to fish and it requires bait in the well, but it's been worth the extra effort this week.

White marlin have shown too, scattered rather than stacked — a fish here, a double there, mostly picked up on the smaller ballyhoo and squid chains worked closer to the surface temp break where the water's cleanest. It hasn't been a bill-fish bonanza, more a bonus when the conditions line up right on top of a good tuna push. Worth running a couple of dedicated marlin lures — a pink-and-white Ilander or a small Moldcraft — off the long riggers if you're already committed to trolling the break; no reason to leave that opportunity on the table.

Wahoo and mahi have been the wildcard. Neither has been consistent, but boats running high-speed trolling gear — planers and wire line pulling Yo-Zuri or Braid lures in the 12-15 knot range along structure edges — have picked off a wahoo or two on days the current was really moving. Mahi have mostly shown as incidental catches around any floating debris or weed lines inside the canyon rather than a dedicated target this week.

The why here is straightforward. That warm filament pushing down from the Gulf Stream has set up a hard temperature edge over the canyon, and that edge is doing exactly what it does this time of year — concentrating bait against the break and pulling everything up the food chain in behind it. When that edge is sharp and stable, as it's been, the fish sit tight to it and the bite holds. When it softens or slides, the fish scatter toward the drop-offs and the deeper edges of the canyon, which is the scenario worth watching for over the next several days.

Looking ahead, the next 24 to 48 hours should look a lot like the last week if the filament holds — steady jig bite on the bigeye over structure, giants workable on the troll and live bait, marlin as a bonus rather than a target. The bigger variable is the new moon tide arriving September 10. That's typically a pivot point for bait movement coastwide, and out here it could either tighten up the bait even more against the break — which would be good news for anyone planning a run late this week — or start to loosen things up if the tide change works against the eddy's current position. Either way, run out with a plan for both troll and chunk, keep an eye on the latest temp data before committing to a spot, and don't be afraid to switch tactics mid-day if the marks on the sounder tell you to.

Fuel math matters here too. This isn't a close-in day trip — it's a long run, and burning gas on a guess is a bad way to fish the Wilmington. If the temp break looks textbook when you clear the inlet, commit to it. If it's fuzzy or you're not seeing bait, better to work the edges methodically than to burn the tank chasing yesterday's report.
